description: Meursault does not cry at his mother's funeral. Camus invents the absurd in 123 radically dry pages.

hero.hook: “Today, mom died. » A simple sentence. A trial for anything other than murder.

blocks.text: **The Stranger**, published in **1942**, is the first novel by**Albert Camus**. In **123 pages** of **white writing**, neutral and unadorned style, it follows **Meursault**, an office worker in Algiers whose indifference to social conventions leads him to his downfall.

The book fictionalizes the . The absurd is born from the clash between our desire for meaning and the silence of the world. Meursault does not cheat with his emotions: it is precisely this refusal that condemns him. **[[The absurd in Camus]]**

**Albert Camus** grew up in , French Algeria in the 1930s, in a modest family marked by silence. He develops the cycle of the absurd: the novel **The Stranger**, the essay **The Myth of Sisyphus** and the play **Caligula**. **[[Colonial Algeria as context]]**

blocks.caption: Albert Camus: lucidity, revolt and refusal to cheat.

blocks.text: For Camus, the absurd does not lead to nihilism, the belief that nothing has meaning, but to **revolt**: living despite the absence of transcendent meaning. The novel was published by , a prestigious Parisian publishing house, in the midst of **Occupation**, France under Nazi domination. Camus expresses an ethic of lucidity in a world in crisis. **[[Gallimard]]**

sections.title: Camus and the cycle of the absurd

blocks.text: Meursault refuses to lie about his feelings, both at his mother's funeral and in front of **Married**, his friend. He experiences the present and its physical sensations, heat, light, fatigue, more than the morality imposed by society. His behavior shocks because he does not play the expected role of the grieving son.

blocks.caption: The beach of Algiers: overwhelming light, trigger of the drama.

blocks.text: In Algerian French of the time, “mama” was a common term of affection, devoid of the childish connotation it carries in mainland France.

Dazzled by the sun on a beach, Meursault shoots an “Arab” whose name the text leaves out. The gesture is neither hatred nor revenge, but a tragic coincidence. This absence of name has nourished  readings, critical analyzes of colonization and its representations. **[[postcolonial]]**

sections.title: Meursault: the man without a mask

blocks.text: The trial does not only judge the murder. The prosecutor accuses Meursault of having drunk café au lait in front of his mother's coffin and of going to the cinema the next day. Society condemns anyone who refuses collective mourning rituals. The novel shows that public morality can be harsher than criminal justice.

blocks.attribution: Albert Camus, The Stranger — first sentence
blocks.text: Today, mom died. Or maybe yesterday, I don't know.

Meursault will be executed for having “buried his mother with the heart of a criminal”. Facing the chaplain, he claims his life and accepts the “tender indifference of the world”. He finds a form of peace in lucidity.

**Jean-Paul Sartre** explains the importance of chopped style in the first person. The novel announces the **[[New Novel]]**, current in the 1950s which breaks the conventions of the story. The **[[postcolonial]]** studies question the anonymity of the victim, reread by, Algerian writer, in “Meursault, counter-investigation”. **[[Kamel Daoud]]**

blocks.text: Camus is not writing a philosophy textbook. It shows a man who refuses ready-made sentences, to the point of paying the price. Sun, beach, trial: each concrete detail prepares a broader question about the meaning of life. The novel remains one of the most translated texts of the 20th century, read as much for its style as for its ideas.
**The Stranger** illustrates the **[[The absurd in Camus]]**: Meursault is condemned less for his crime than for his refusal to simulate emotions imposed by society.
